newsitem.title: USA: AFL-CIO political drive produces mixed results.
newsitem.headline: AFL-CIO political drive produces mixed results.

text.p: The American labour movement's unprecedented $35 million drive to unseat unfriendly lawmakers produced mixed results as most of the targeted Republicans survived the advertising blitzes against them.

The AFL-CIO saw its dreaded Republican majority in the Senate widen slightly, but could take a bit of solace in the fact that Democrats gained a few seats in the House, but not enough to take away control from the Republicans.
The election results left officials of the 78-union federation reluctant to talk. Instead they issued a statement to highlight the few comforting nuggets in the election that they could find.
"Although they retained control of Congress, Republicans lost the popular vote 48 to 50 percent," AFL-CIO President John Sweeney said in the prepared statement.
The AFL-CIO campaign, its most ambitious political undertaking ever, sparked stinging counterattacks from Republicans and business groups.

Citing statistics that in the overall political arena, business outspends organised labour by seven-to-one, Sweeney said labour was nevertheless responsible this time for setting an agenda for the elections that included Medicare, pensions, education and health care.
"The 105th Congress will legislate under the spotlight of a working families agenda, not a business-driven Contract with America," he said, referring to the House Republicans' uniting banner of 1994.
Of the 30 mostly freshman Republican members of the House who bore the brunt of the media campaign arranged by the AFL-CIO, 18 were re-elected, 11 lost and one race remains up in the air.
And in 102 congressional districts, including those 30, where the labour federation deployed coordinators and activists to get out the union vote, only 19 of labour's enemies lost.

In all no more than 15 of the 73 freshmen Republicans, who were despised by organised labour for their conservative stands, were defeated. Another three did not seek re-election to the House but were replaced by other Republicans.
U.S. Chamber of Commerce spokesman Frank Coleman said his group was "jubilant" with the overall results.
"We preserved the first pro-business congressional majority in anyone's memory," said Coleman.
Bruce Josten, a senior vice president of the Chamber, who assembled 33 business groups to wage a counteroffensive media campaign against the AFL-CIO, said labour's tactics backfired.
"I don't believe the American people want their intelligence insulted with disinformation campaigns," he said. "I think at the end of the day Sweeney's credibility went down."

Josten's group, "The Coalition," raised only $5 million for its ad campaign, compared with the $25 million raised by the AFL-CIO for advertising and $10 million for other election activities, mostly get-out-the-vote drives. The figures exclude election spending by other unions, firms and business groups.
Josten said the AFL-CIO media campaign may have energised union members, "but I don't think he won the hearts and minds of the American people."

The AFL-CIO campaign, which was approved by all of its member unions last March, was intended to highlight the positions of incumbant lawmakers on a range of issues deemed important to working people, in an effort to focus attention away from "hot button" issus such as abortion and gun control. The ads did not advocate the election of any candidate.

Despite failing to oust the Republican majority in the House, Sweeney's statement credited the federation's efforts with raising union household participation in the election to 23 percent from 19 percent in 1992 and 14 percent in 1994.
He also said that only 35 percent of union household voters chose Republican congressional candidates this year, down from 40 percent in 1994, while 62 percent voted Democratic.
In the presidential race, Sweeney said 59 percent of union household voters went with President Bill Clinton, while 29 percent voted for Republican Bob Dole.
